Neurons as autonomous agents: : A biologically inspired framework for cognitive architectures in artificial intelligence

Neurons can be seen as agents pursuing the supreme goal of producing "useful" signals, which incentivizes optimized connectivity (with neighbors that represent complementary features) and firing patterns and is rewarded via nutrients, plasticity, and neuromodulation.

Neurons as agents

Researchers like Michael Levin and Daniel Dennett argue that we should view every neuron as an autonomous agent, albeit a tiny one, that pursues basic objectives (such as survival, homeostasis, and influence) within the neural economy.

This perspective, sometimes called "basal cognition" or the "neurons as agents" view, recognizes that neurons descend from free-living single cells and have retained a degree of independence and "know-how." Dennett notes that every neuron is a direct descendant of unicellular organisms that "lived and fended for themselves for about a billion years as free-living little agents", evolving robust self-preservation strategies. In multicellular brains, neurons are "domesticated" as part of a larger organism, yet may still exhibit a feral streak - competing and cooperating like selfish agents within the brain’s internal ecosystem 2. A 2025 computational study explores energy objectives in spiking neurons (Figure). The model compares expected and unexpected inputs (Figure).

On this view, a neuron’s goal is not explicitly defined by any central controller; rather, each neuron tries to "stay alive" and useful by embedding itself in circuits where it gets sufficient inputs neuromodulatory rewards. If a neuron falls idle (receives too little input or activation), it risks losing vital resources and even dying. This creates an intrinsic drive for neurons to seek activity - effectively an internal competition for signals and survival. For example, in a classic experiment, Merzenich sutured two fingers of a monkey together, reducing distinct sensory input to the cortex. Neurons in the monkey’s cortical map that no longer received separate inputs rapidly reorganized their connections (shrinking the unused representation and expanding into new functions). Similarly, when researchers blindfolded humans for weeks, neurons in the visual cortex quickly began responding to touch and Braille, effectively retraining themselves to remain useful in processing information.

As Dennett puts it, "Why should these idle neurons be so eager to pitch in? Well, they’re out of work... pretty soon you’re going to die." In other words, neurons that lose their role will aggressively seek a new role - a striking demonstration of agent-like behavior at the cellular level. The brain thus contains an internal economy where neurons compete and form alliances for functionality, which underlies the brain’s plasticity and reorganization capacity.

The agency of neurons is not a mystical claim but a shift in explanatory framework; Levin and colleagues suggest that adopting an intentional stance toward cells - thinking of them as if they have preferences or goals - can yield better insights in biology. 3

Neurons exhibit homeostatic regulations that resemble simple goal-directed behaviors: they maintain their firing rates within an optimal range, adjust ion channels and synapses to stabilize activity, and seek out proper connections. These can be seen as each neuron’s homeostatic goal to preserve its functional role. Indeed, in Levin’s view, there is a continuum of cognition and agency from single cells up to whole organisms; his "cognitive light cone" concept quantifies intelligence by the spatio-temporal scale of the largest goal an agent can pursue. Bacteria pursue small spatial and temporal goals around local sugar concentrations, while neurons maintain medium-scale goals for signal propagation and synaptic maintenance. Neural networks coordinate large-scale goals for pattern recognition and behavior, with organisms pursuing very large-scale goals including survival and long-term planning.

Viewing the brain as an economy of agents leads to various insights:

It clarifies why prediction is baked into neural computation, rather than being an add-on algorithm sitting "above" the hardware. If a neuron’s survival depends on securing scarce metabolic resources, the safest strategy is to fire only when its future activity will still be rewarded-i.e., when its output will prove useful to its partners. Luczak and colleagues formalized that survival calculus and showed that maximizing a single cell’s future energy balance forces it to become a local predictor and to update synapses so as to minimize its own surprise; networks built from so-called "lazy" neurons spontaneously develop canonical prediction-error dynamics that look like cortical mismatch responses 4. Independent modeling work goes further: when a spiking network is trained under a combined "do the task and save ATP" objective, predictive-coding motifs (distinct driver and error units, suppression of expected inputs, etc.) emerge without being hard-wired, suggesting that what we call "predictive coding" may simply be the ecological outcome of billions of tiny agents economizing energy 5.

It turns classical plasticity into an evolutionary "market." Synapses and dendritic branches are no longer just signal paths; they are investments. Active synapses draw more glucose, oxygen, and molecular building blocks, whereas inactive ones wither. Recent reviews of "synaptic logistics" document direct competition for ribosomes, trafficking motors, and even local blood flow; neurons and their synapses vie for these limited supplies much as organisms compete for food 6. Whole-brain synaptic scaling acts like a centralized price-control mechanism in the neural "plasticity market." When global activity drifts too high, the scaling rule proportionally weakens all excitatory synapses, lowering their collective "cost" and freeing metabolic resources. When activity sinks too low, it strengthens synapses across the board, raising their value so that even weaker connections can "afford" the proteins and energy they need. In this way, synaptic scaling prevents any one set of neurons from monopolizing resources while still letting individual synapses compete locally for finer-grained adjustments-keeping every neuronal agent active enough to survive without letting the entire network overheat. A 2024 study investigates competition among dendritic spines (Figure) 7. The study compares observed spine dynamics with resource-competition models (Figure).

The agent lens demystifies the brain’s breathtaking plasticity. When Michael Merzenich sutured two digits of a monkey’s hand, the idle cortical territory was quickly invaded by neurons representing adjacent fingers; those "out-of-work" cells literally sought new jobs to keep nutrient inflow coming. In humans blindfolded for only five days, primary visual cortex is recruited for Braille discrimination and then relinquishes the territory once vision returns-exactly the behavior one would expect from agents scrambling not to lose their metabolic paycheck. Even REM sleep and dreaming can be reinterpreted as neurons in the visual system staging a nightly "occupancy drill" to prevent other senses from annexing their turf.

It sharpens our understanding of neuromodulators and vascular coupling. From the agent standpoint, dopamine, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine are not abstract teaching signals but global currencies that stabilize the winners of local competitions. A burst of dopamine in motor cortex, for instance, locks in the synapses that just promoted a rewarded action, effectively paying those neurons for valuable work. Conversely, new optical-genetic data show single cortical axons dilating their own arterioles through synapse-like contacts, literally opening the nutrient taps on demand-an elegant example of neurons negotiating their resource budget directly with the vasculature.

Because failures of survival economics can now be targeted, the agent view also reframes disease. Neurodegeneration appears when cells lose the ability to secure enough trophic support; epilepsy resembles an arms race in which excitatory agents succeed too well and overwhelm the inhibitory economy; certain psychiatric syndromes can be cast as breakdowns in the neuromodulatory currency that normally adjudicates competition. By treating neurons as self-interested actors, these conditions become market-design problems-suggesting therapies that restore fair resource allocation rather than merely dampening activity.
